                                            A LAZARD-TYPE CORRESPONDENCE AND APPLICATIONS
                                                   TO SKEW BRACES AND POST-LIE RINGS

                                                                                S. TRAPPENIERS


                                                   Abstract. Through a Hopf algebraic approach, we develop a framework for
                                                   formal differentiation and integration and prove a correspondence theorem
arXiv:2406.02475v1 [math.RA] 4 Jun 2024




                                                   that comprises the Lazard correspondence, the Malcev correspondence and
                                                   the formal integration of complete connected Lie algebras with characteristic
                                                   0. We then apply this theory to obtain a correspondence theorem for classes
                                                   of left nilpotent skew braces on a nilpotent group and left nilpotent post-Lie
                                                   rings on a nilpotent Lie ring.




                                                                               1. Introduction
                                             In 1954, Lazard proved a correspondence between Lie rings and groups satisfying
                                          certain completeness conditions [21]. The nowadays better known version of this,
                                          although more restrictive than the original version, states that for pk a prime power,
                                          there is a bijective correspondence between nilpotent Lie rings of order pk and
                                          nilpotency class at most p − 1, and nilpotent groups of order pk of nilpotency
                                          class at most p − 1. In particular, one finds a correspondence between groups of
                                          order pk and nilpotent Lie rings of order pk for k < p. This has proved to be
                                          very useful in the classification of finite p-groups, see for example [25]. Lazard’s
                                          ideas built upon earlier work by Malcev [22], who proved a correspondence between
                                          nilpotent rational Lie algebras and nilpotent radicable torsionfree groups. Quillen
                                          extended Malcev’s result to arbitrary field of characteristic 0 [28], his technique is
                                          now generally referred to as formal integration.
                                             Pre-Lie algebras, also called left-symmetric algebras, arose as early as in 1881
                                          in the work of Cayley [11], only to resurface again 80 years later in the works of
                                          Vinberg [40] and Koszul [20]. See [9] for a survey on pre-Lie algebras. One of
                                          the motivations to study pre-Lie algebras comes from geometry, as they appear
                                          naturally in the study of regular affine actions of Lie groups [19]. More recently,
                                          the notion of a post-Lie algebra was introduced in the works of Valette [39], see also
                                          [15]. For R a commutative ring, a post-Lie R-algebra is a Lie R-algebra a together
                                          with an R-bilinear map ⊲ : a × a → a satisfying:
                                          (1.1)                        x ⊲ [y, z] = [x ⊲ y, z] + [y, x ⊲ z],
                                          (1.2)                        [x, y] ⊲ z = (x, y, z)⊲ − (y, x, z)⊲ ,
                                          with (x, y, z)⊲ := x ⊲ (y ⊲ z) − (x ⊲ y) ⊲ z. If a is abelian, then (a, ⊲) is a pre-Lie
                                          R-algebra. A post-Lie Z-algebra, respectively pre-Lie Z-algebra is called a post-Lie
                                          ring, respectively pre-Lie ring.
                                             Braces were introduced in 2006 by Rump [29, 30] in the study of the set-
                                          theoretical Yang–Baxter equation. They were subsequently generalized by Guarnieri
                                          and Vendramin to skew braces [18]. A skew brace is a triple (A, ·, ◦) with A a set

                                              2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. 17B69, 20N99, 20F19, 20F40.
                                              Key words and phrases. post-Lie algebra, pre-Lie algebra, brace, skew brace, left nilpotent,
                                          nilpotent group, Lazard correspondence.
                                                                                         1
2                                   S. TRAPPENIERS


and (A, ·) and (A, ◦) group structures such that
                           a ◦ (b · c) = (a ◦ b) · a−1 · (a ◦ b),
holds for all a, b, c ∈ A. Here a−1 denotes the inverse of a in (A, ·). When (A, ·)
is abelian, then (A, ·, ◦) is called a brace. For braces, the notation (A, +, ◦) is also
common (in fact, this is also the case for skew braces, but to avoid any possible
confusion we will abstain from using + for a non-abelian group operation). Skew
braces are essentially the same as bijective 1-cocycles of groups or regular subgroups
of the holomorph of a group. In this sense, they have already been studied in a
geometric framework in the form of regular affine actions of Lie groups on vector
spaces [3, 24] long before their current definition. Since pre-Lie algebras played
an important role there, some connection between skew braces and pre-Lie rings is
to be expected. This was indeed first stated by Rump [31] for R-braces, he also
gave an idea of how to use the Lazard correspondence for the finite case. Bachiller
then used techniques similar to the ones that Rump alluded to in order to give
a counterexample of a conjecture on braces [4], starting from a counterexample
by Burde [8] to a question by Milnor [24] (note that the first counterexample to
Milnor’s question was given earlier by Benoist [6]).
   Smoktunowicz proved that the construction of the group of flows, as defined
for pre-Lie algebras in [2], could be adapted to left nilpotent pre-Lie rings of prime
power order pk , with k +1 < p, in order to obtain braces [36] with the same additive
structure. Here, a post-Lie algebra (a, ⊲) is left nilpotent if there exists some n such
that an = 0 where a1 = a and ai+1 is the subgroup of (a, +) generated by a ⊲ b
for a ∈ a, b ∈ ai , right nilpotency is defined analogously. Similarly, a skew brace
(A, ·, ◦) is left nilpotent if there exists some n such that An = 1, where A1 = A and
Ai+1 is the subgroup of (A, ·) generated by the elements a ∗ b = a−1 · (a ◦ b) · b−1
for all a ∈ A, b ∈ Ai , right nilpotency is defined analogously. Recall that a skew
brace of prime power order is always left nilpotent [12]. It is not immediately clear
whether this construction is invertible, as only an inverse construction is given
in the case of strongly nilpotent braces of order pk , with k + 1 < p, and with
strong nilpotency index at most p − 1. Here strong nilpotency is equivalent to the
structures being both left and right nilpotent [33]. This correspondence was used
to classify all strongly nilpotent braces of order p4 , for p > 55 , in [26] while the
non-strongly nilpotent ones were classified earlier in [27]. In [35], a construction is
given starting from a brace (A, +, ◦) of order pk , with k + 1 < p, in order to obtain
a pre-Lie ring structure with additive group (A, +)/{a ∈ A | p2 a = 0}. Although
the strong nilpotency condition is no longer present, one can not hope that this
yields a correspondence as we quotient by a non-trivial subgroup.
   Recently, Bai, Guo, Sheng and Tang showed how from a regular affine action of
a Lie group onto another Lie group, one obtains a post-Lie algebra through differ-
entiation [5] (note that, although not explicitly stated in this way, this construction
also appears in [10]). This extended the earlier techniques to obtain a pre-Lie al-
gebra in the case that the latter group is Rn . Conversely, also in [5] a construction
by formal integration was given which yields a skew brace structure starting from
a post-Lie algebra of characteristic 0 and with some completeness conditions.
   A common idea is present in the earlier mentioned works of Malcev, Lazard and
Quillen: starting from a Lie ring g we want to embed it into an algebra A, moreover
the exponential and logarithmic map exp and log should be defined on (subsets of)
A and in this way exp(g) is a group (with some additional structure). This group
structure is then transferred onto a since log(exp(a)) = a. The first goal of this
paper is to introduce a general theory where precisely this idea can be applied.
The second goal is then to define post-Lie algebras and skew braces in this context
and give a uniform treatment of formal differentiation and integration, yielding a
           LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE, SKEW BRACES AND POST-LIE RINGS                         3


correspondence between these two structures. The exact definitions can be found
in the respective sections, but the following overview should give a general intuition
as to how we approach this. In particular, note that the analogy with the approach
taken in [28, 41].
    In Section 2 we introduce the main actors of this paper, i.e. sequences of rings
R and modules over such sequences. We prove the necessary properties of this
category of modules which allow us to define R-algebras, Lie R-algebras, co R-
algebras and Hopf R-algebras.
    We next proceed in Section 3 to prove that if R has a certain divisibility property,
then the Poincarré-Birkhoff-Witt theorem holds in our context.
    By introducing a completion operation in Section 4 we can then also obtain
the Poincarré-Birkhoff-Witt theorem in the complete setting and moreover also the
Milnor-Moore theorem is proved under the earlier divisibility condition on R.
    In Section 5, we then introduce the notion of an R-group. They are naturally
obtained as the grouplike elements of a (complete) Hopf R-algebra. By defining the
exponential and logarithmic map on complete Hopf R-algebras we are able to obtain
a Lazard-type correspondence between complete Lie R-algebras and complete R-
groups under some natural conditions.
    In Section 6 and Section 7 we introduce the notion of post-Lie R-algebras and
skew R-braces. In particular, we prove if (A, ·, ◦) is a left nilpotent skew brace and
(A, ·) is a nilpotent group, then also (A, ◦) is a nilpotent group. This result was
previously only known for finite skew braces [12, Theorem 4.8]. In fact we have a
stronger result, for which we first have to introduce a new notion of nilpotency.
    Let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew brace, define inductively L1 (A) = A and Li+1 (A) the
subgroup of (A, ·) generated by all elements of the form a ∗ b = a−1 · (a ◦ b) · b−1 and
a · b · a−1 · b−1 for a ∈ A, b ∈ Li (A). Note Li (A) is the left hand version of the series
Rn (A, A) as defined in [1]. By induction, one sees that the Li (A) are a descending
chain of normal subgroups of (A, ·). We now define L-nilpotency of skew braces,
which for braces clearly coincides with left nilpotency.
Definition 1.1. A skew brace (A, ·, ◦) is L-nilpotent if there Lk+1 (A) = 1 for some
k ≥ 0. The minimal such k, if it exists, is the L-nilpotency class of A.
   We can now give a more precise formulation of our results which imply the earlier
claim.
Lemma 1.2. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew brace. Then A is L-nilpotent if and only if A
is left nilpotent and (A, ·) is a nilpotent group.
Theorem 1.3. Let (A, ·, ◦) be an L-nilpotent skew brace of class k. Then (A, ◦) is
nilpotent of class at most k and the k-th term in the lower central series of (A, ◦)
is contained in Ann(A).
   Recall that
                 Soc(A) := {a ∈ A | a ◦ b = a + b = b + a for all b ∈ A},
                 Fix(A) := {a ∈ A | b ◦ a = b + a for all b ∈ A},
              Ann(A) := Soc(A) ∩ Fix(A).
   In Section 8 we first prove that the exp and log give a correspondence between
certain derivations and automorphisms of Lie R-algebras, mimicking the geometric
correspondence given by integration and differentiation. We then prove the cor-
respondence between post-Lie R-algebras and skew R-braces under the necessary
completeness and divisibility condition. In particular, we obtain an extension of
Smoktunowicz’s correspondence on pre-Lie rings and braces of prime power order.
Before formulating this result, we introduce the notion of L-nilpotency.
4                                   S. TRAPPENIERS


   Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie ring. Inductively define L1 (a) = a and Li+1 (a) the
subgroup of (a, +) generated by all elements of the form a ⊲ b and [a, b] where
a ∈ A, b ∈ Li (A). One easily verifies that Li (a) gives a descending filtration of
ideals of the Lie ring a. We now are ready to define L-nilpotency, which for pre-Lie
rings is the same as left nilpotency.
Definition 1.4. A post-Lie ring (a, ⊲) is L-nilpotent if Lk+1 (a) = 0 for some k ≥ 0.
The minimal such k, if it exists, is the L-nilpotency class of (a, ⊲).
  We are now ready to formulate the result, which will follow as a somewhat direct
application of the more technical correspondence in Theorem 8.19.
Theorem 1.5. Let p be a prime and k < p. There is a bijective correspondence
between post-Lie rings (a, ⊲) of L-nilpotency class k such that (a, +) is a p-group
and skew braces (A, ·, ◦) of L-nilpotency class k such that (A, ·) is a p-group.
   In particular, there is a bijective correspondence between skew braces of size pk
and L-nilpotent post-Lie rings of size pk .
   This correspondence is explicitly described in Proposition 8.14 and Proposi-
tion 8.17. The proof of Theorem 1.5 is given at the end of Section 8.
   We further discuss how our notion of completeness relates to the classical notion
of completeness for finite dimensional pre-Lie algebras defined in [19] and to the
notion of completeness as coined in [5] and how our constructions related to the
ones in [2, 5, 36].
   In [5] the authors propose to find a suitable differentiation and formal integra-
tion theory for finite skew braces and post-Lie rings. On the one hand, the idea of
considering the logarithm of function as a differentiation, which is the principal ap-
proach in this paper, does prove to be fruitful. On the other hand, some techniques
used by Smoktunowicz in [34, 36] could also be seen as an discrete version of differ-
entiation. Therefore, in Section 9 we motivate why this is the case and we give an
application to skew braces that extends an application by Smoktunowicz. We end
by emphasizing a possible advantage of this technique and ask whether this could
possibly lead to a relaxation on the nilpotency condition imposed by the exponent
of the group in [36, Theorem 13]. In particular, this could lead to applications to
braces of size 2k , whereas up until now all of the known constructions are trivial
when p = 2.

                         2. The category of R-modules
    In what follows, R will always denote a sequence of commutative rings
                          d0         d1        d2         d3
                    R0         R1         R2         R3        ...

where di : Ri → Ri+1 are ring homomorphisms. All rings are assumed to be unital,
but we do not exclude the case 0 = 1. For a ring R we denote by R the constant
sequence where Ri = R and di = idR for all i ≥ 0.
Definition 2.1. An R-module is an abelian group M with a descending filtration
of subgroups M0 ⊇ M1 ⊇ ... such that for every i ≥ 0, Mi is a Ri -module such that
moreover r ·i m = di (r) ·i+1 m for all r ∈ Ri and m ∈ Mi+1 .
   An R-submodule N of an R-module M is a subgroup of M with filtration Ni =
N ∩ Mi such that Ni is a Ri -submodule of Mi for all i ≥ 0. Given a submodule N
we define the quotient module M/N as the quotient M/N (as an abelian group)
with filtration (M/N )i = (Mi + N )/N and the natural R-module structure coming
from the isomorphism (Mi + N )/N ∼    = Mi /(N ∩ Mi ).
          LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE, SKEW BRACES AND POST-LIE RINGS                        5


   A homomorphism of R-modules is a map f : M → N such that for all i ≥ 0,
f (Mi ) ⊆ Ni and the restrictions f : Mi → Ni are Ri -module homomorphisms. The
ring of all R-module homomorphisms of M is denoted EndR (M ).
   The category of R-modules is denoted R Mod.
   Note that because of the compatibility condition, we can denote all module
actions by juxtaposition without any possible confusion. Another way to see an R-
module is as follows: Let M be an abelian group with a descending filtration. For
i ≥ 0, define Endf (Mi ) as all group endomorphisms of Mi which map Mj into itself
for j ≥ i, hence we get restriction maps Endf (Mi ) → Endf (Mi+1 ). An R-module
is then a family of ring homomorphisms (ρi : Ri → Endf (Mi ))i≥0 such that the
following diagram commutes.
                            d0                 d1              d2
                  R0                R1                 R2            ...
                    ρ0                ρ1                ρ2

               End(M0 )          End(M1 )           End(M2 )         ...

Example 2.2. For R a ring, an R-module is simply a filtered R-module.
Example 2.3. Given an Ri module M , for some i ≥ 0, we can make M into an
R-module by setting Mj = M for j ≤ i and Mj = 0 for j > i. For j ≤ i, r ∈ Rj
and m ∈ M we then define rm = di−1 . . . dj (r)m. In particular, this makes the
rings Ri themselves into R-modules.
Example 2.4. Let R∞ be the direct limit of the sequence R. Then similar to the
previous example the ring homomorphisms Ri → R∞ give R∞ a natural R-module
structure where R∞ where the filtration is constant.
Lemma 2.5. Let (Mj )j∈J be a family of R-modules.
                                            Q        Then the           (Mj )j∈J
                                                           Q product of Q
in the category R Mod exists and is given by j∈J Mj where ( j∈J Mj )i = j∈J (Mj )i
and the R-structure is defined componentwise. AlsoQ the coproduct of (Mj )j∈J in
the category R Mod exists and is the submodule of j∈J Mj of elements with finite
                          L
support, which we denote j∈J Mj .
Definition 2.6. A filtered set is a set X together with a filtration X0 ⊇ X1 ⊇
X2 ⊇ .... A map f : X → Y between filtered sets is a homomorphism if f (Xi ) ⊆ Yi
for all i ≥ 0. The category of filtered sets is denoted Setf .
  For X a filtered set, we define the degree function deg : X → N ∪ {∞} as
deg(x) = sup{i ≥ 0 | x ∈ Xi }.
Lemma 2.7. The forgetful functor R Mod → Setf : M 7→ M admits a left adjoint.
Proof. For a filtered set X consider the R-module
                                       M
                               RX =       Rdeg(x) x,
                                         x∈X

where Ri and R∞ are given the R-module structure as in Example 2.3 and Ex-
ample 2.4. One easily checks that this defines a functor that is left adjoint to the
forgetful functor R Mod → Setf .                                                  

Definition 2.8. A homomorphism of filtered sets f : X → Y is
   (1) degree preserving if f −1 (Yi ) = Xi for all i ≥ 0. Note that this is equivalent
       to deg(m) = deg(f (m)) for all x ∈ X.
   (2) a regular surjection if the restriction fi : Xi → Yi is surjective for all i ≥ 0.
6                                   S. TRAPPENIERS


    Regular surjections are important since in the category R Mod it is not true that
every bijective homomorphism f : M → N is an isomorphism. Indeed, the inverse
map f −1 is only a homomorphism of R-modules if f −1 (Ni ) ⊆ Mi for all i ≥ 0, so
if f is regular.
Lemma 2.9. Let f : M → N be a homomorphism of R-modules. Then the follow-
ing are equivalent:
    (1) f is an isomorphism,
    (2) f is an injective regular surjection.
Definition 2.10. Let M, N, P be R-modules. A map b : M × N → P is bilinear if
    (1) b(Mi , Nj ) ⊆ Pi+j for all i, j ≥ 0,
    (2) The maps
                           b(−, n) : M → P : m 7→ b(m, n),
        and
                           b(m, −) : N → P : n 7→ b(m, n),
        are R-module homomorphisms for every m ∈ M, n ∈ N .
Proposition 2.11. Let M, N be R-modules, there exists an R-module M ⊗ N and
bilinear map ⊗ : M ×N → M ⊗N such that for every R-module P and bilinear map
b : M × N → P , there exists a unique R-module homomorphism b : M ⊗ N → P
such that b = b⊗.
                                                       S
Proof. Consider the set X = M × N with filtration Xk = i+j=k Mi × Nj and let
F = RX. We define M ⊗ N as F/I where I is the R-submodule of F generated by
              {(m1 + m2 , n) − (m1 , n) − (m2 , n) | m1 , m2 ∈ M, n ∈ N }
              ∪{(m, n1 + n2 ) − (m, n1 ) − (m, n2 ) | m ∈ M, n1 , n2 ∈ N }
                    ∪{r(m, n) − (rm, n) | r ∈ Ri , m ∈ Mi , n ∈ N }
                   ∪{r(m, n) − (m, rn) | r ∈ Rj , m ∈ M, n ∈ Nj }.
It is now easily seen that the universal property is satisfied.                    

  As usual, for m ∈ M, n ∈ N we will denote the image ⊗(m, n) in M ⊗ N as
m ⊗ n. We can define sM,N : M ⊗ N → N ⊗ M as the R-linear map such that
sM,N (m ⊗ n) = n ⊗ m. It is straightforward to verify the following proposition.
Proposition 2.12. (R Mod, ⊗, R0 , s) is symmetric monoidal additive category.
Definition 2.13. Consider the symmetric monoidal additive category (R Mod, ⊗, R0 , s),
    (1) an monoid in this category is called an R-algebra. We denote the category
        of R-algebras by R Alg.
    (2) a comonoid in this category is called a co R-algebra. The comultiplication
        and the counit of a co R-algebra will be denoted by ∆ and ε. When
        evaluating ∆ in specific elements, we will use Sweedler notation.
    (3) a Lie algebra object in this category is called a Lie R-algebra. We denote
        the category of Lie R-algebras by R Lie.
    (4) a Hopf monoid in this category is called a Hopf R-algebra. We denote the
        category of Hopf R-algebras by R Hopf. The antipode of a Hopf R-algebra
        we be denoted by S.
Example 2.14. Considering the original ring structure on the R-module R0 makes
it into an R-algebra.
          LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE, SKEW BRACES AND POST-LIE RINGS                       7


Example 2.15. Let H be a filtered algebra (in the classical sense) over some field F,
then H is an F-algebra. Note that every algebra can be made into a filtered algebra
by choosing the constant filtration. The same construction applies to (filtered) Lie
and Hopf-algebras over fields.
Example 2.16. Let M be an R-module. The ring EndR (M ) of R-linear endo-
morphisms of M has a natural filtration given by
                   EndR (M )i = {f | f (Mj ) ⊆ Mj+i for all j ≥ 0},
and a natural R-module structure given by (rf )(m) = rf (m) for all r ∈ Ri , f ∈
EndR (M )i and m ∈ M . This makes EndR (M ) into an R-algebra.
   Let H be a Hopf R-algebra H. An element x ∈ H is primitive if ∆(x) =
1⊗x+x⊗1. The set of primitive elements of H is denoted P(H). One easily verifies
that P(H) is a sub R-module of H and that the operation [x, y] = xy − yx makes
P H into a Lie R-algebra. In this way we obtain a functor P : R Hopf → R Lie.
   Given M ∈ R Mod,
                  L∞ define      T 0 (M ) = R0 and T i+1 (M ) = M ⊗ T i (M ). We
                           i
consider T (M ) = i=0 T (M ) as an R-algebra with the canonical multiplication
and unit. One easily verifies the following property.
Proposition 2.17. The functor R Mod → R Alg : M 7→ T (M ) is left adjoint to
the functor P : R Alg → R Mod : H 7→ H.
    It follows directly from Proposition 2.17 that there exists a unique R-algebra
homomorphism ∆ : T (M ) → T (M ) ⊗ T (M ) satisfying ∆(m) = m ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ m. Let
ε : T (M ) → R0 be the projection onto T 0 (M ) = R0 , and let S : T (M ) → T (M ) be
the unique anti-automorphism such that S(m) = −m for m ∈ M . Considering this
extra structure on T (M ) is easily seen to make it into a (co-commutative) Hopf
R-algebra which satisfies the following property.
Proposition 2.18. The functor R Mod → R Hopf : M 7→ T (M ) is left adjoint to
the functor P : R Hopf → R Mod : H 7→ P(H).
Proposition 2.19. The functor P : R Hopf → R Lie admits a left adjoint U :
R Lie → R Hopf .

Proof. Let g be a Lie R-algebra and let I be the ideal of T (g) generated by
                          {x ⊗ y − y ⊗ x − [x, y] | x, y ∈ L}.
Then I is a Hopf ideal as ∆(x ⊗ y − y ⊗ x − [x, y]) ∈ I ⊗ T (L) + T (L) ⊗ I and
S(x ⊗ y − y ⊗ x − [x, y]) = y ⊗ x − x ⊗ y − [y, x] ∈ I. We define U(g) = T (g)/I.
This construction is easily seen to be functorial and from the universal property of
T (g) it follows that also U(g) satisfies the required universal property.        
Example 2.20. Let M be an R-module and consider it as an abelian Lie R-algebra.
We define S(M ) = U(M ), hence S(M ) = T (M )/I with I the Lideal generated by

                         3. Divisible sequences of rings
Definition 3.1. A sequence of commutative rings R is said to be divisible if k is
invertible in Rk for every k > 0.
Example 3.2. Let Q0 = Z and for i ≥ 1 let Qk denote the subring of Q consisting
            n
of fraction m where all prime divisors of m are at most k. So
                        n                          n
        Q1 = Z, Q2 = { k | n ∈ Z, k ∈ N}, Q3 = { k l | n ∈ Z, k, l ∈ N}, . . .
                       2                         2 3
8                                       S. TRAPPENIERS


Then Q : Q0 → Q1 → Q2 → . . . is a divisible sequence of rings, where all homo-
morphisms are simply the inclusion.
   It is easily seen that for R a divisible sequence, there exist unique homomor-
phisms ιi : Qi → Ri compatible with the maps of Q and R. Hence, every R-module
is a Q-module.

Example 3.3. Let R be a ring of non-zero characteristic and let p denote the
smallest prime number dividing char R. Note that 1, ..., p − 1 are invertible in R
but p is not. We define Re as the sequence R0 = ... = Rp−1 = R and 0 = Rp = ...
with di = idR for 0 ≤ i < p − 1. Then Re is a divisible sequence and R-modules
                                                                     e          are
precisely the R-modules M such that Mp = 0.

Definition 3.4. A filtered set X is connected if X0 = X1 . An R-module or Lie
R-algebra is connected if its underlying filtered set is connected. A Hopf R-algebra
H is connected if H1 = ker ε.

    We are now able to prove the Poincarré-Birkhoff-Witt theorem in our setting.

Theorem 3.5. Let R be divisible and g a connected Lie R-algebra. Then there
exists an isomorphism of co R-algebras φ : S(g) → U (g) and φ restricted to g =
S 1 (g) is the canonical map.

Proof. We denote the symmetric group on {1, . . . , k} as Σk . For readability, we also
write S = S(g), T i = T i (g) and T = T (g). Consider the R-linear homomorphism
                                                   1 X
                    ψ : S → T : x1 · · · xk 7→         xσ(1) · · · xσ(k) ,
                                                   k!
                                                      σ∈Σk

which is well-defined as any product of k elements in L is contained in Tk and k
is invertible in Rk . We also use the notation σ(x1 · · · xk ) = xσ(1) · · · xσ(k) , and we
extend this linearly to obtain an action of Σk on T k .
    Let I denote the ideal of T (g) generated by {xy − yx − [x, y] | x, y ∈ L}. We

                            4. Complete Hopf R-algebras
   We can naturally consider an R-module M as a topological space where the
base of the topology is given by {m + Mi | m ∈ M, i ≥ 0}. With this topology,
homomorphism of R-modules are automatically continuous. Note that if Mi = 0
for some i, then we obtain the discrete topology on M .
                                                  T∞
Definition 4.1. An R-module M is complete if i=0 Mi = 0 and it is complete
with respect to the above topology. The full subcategory of R Mod consisting of
complete R-modules is denoted R Modc .
     One easily verifies that
        (                                ∞

 M is complete then M ∼        = M̂ . This construction can easily be extended to a functor

 we define M ⊗N   ˆ as M    \  ⊗ N.
 Proposition 4.2. The category (R Modc , R0 , ⊗,       ˆ ŝ) is a symmetric monoidal addi-
 tive category and the functor ˆ· : R Mod → R Modc is symmetric monoidal additive.
 Proof. We will prove that for any M, N ∈ R Mod, M         \   ⊗ N is canonically isomorphic

     Define M̂ × N̂ → M      \ ⊗ N by mapping ((mi )i , (ni )i )to ((mi ⊗ ni ))i for (mi )i ∈ M̂
 and (ni )i ∈ N̂ which is easily seen to be a well-defined bilinear map of R-modules.
 From the universal property we get a homomorphism g1 : M̂ ⊗ N̂ → (M                \ ⊗ N ) and
 thus also a homomorphism g2 : M̂ ⊗               \
                                           ˆ N̂ → M  ⊗ N.
     Note that the canonical image of M ⊗ N into M       \ ⊗ N is dense. Also its canonical
 image into M̂ ⊗ N̂ is dense, hence the same is true for its canonical image in M̂ ⊗        ˆ N̂ .
 Moreover, on the canonical images of M ⊗ N in M̂ ⊗          ˆ N̂ and M \ ⊗ N , g2 and f2 are
 mutually inverse. Because these canonical images are dense, it follows that f2 and
 g2 are mutually inverse and the desired canonical isomorphism follows.
     It is clear that the R-module R0 is complete and from the definition of ⊗              ˆ it

    A complete R-algebra A is generated by a subset X ⊆ A (which we consider as a
filtered set by setting Xi = X ∩ Ai ) if for each i ≥ 0, Ai is the closed sub R-module

connected Hopf R-algebras is denoted R Hopf c,c      pg . Clearly T̂ (M ) is primitively gen-
erated and connected, and if f : T̂ (M ) → H is a regular surjective homomorphism
of complete Hopf R-algebras, then also H is primitively generated and connected.

The full subcategory of R Liec consisting of complete connected Lie R-algebras is
denoted R Liec,c . We are now ready to prove the Minor-Moore theorem in our
setting.
Theorem 4.7. Let R be divisible, then the functors Û and P define an equivalence
of the categories R Liec,c and R Hopf c,c
                                      pg .

Proof. One easily verifies that we can indeed restrict the functors Û and P to R Liec,c
and R Hopf c,cpg .

by Theorem 4.4 and Lemma 4.5.
    Let H be a primitively generated complete connected Hopf R-algebra, then the
canonical homomorphism of Hopf R-algebras f : Û P(H) → H is a surjection which
is regular as both Hopf R-algebras are primitively generated. The injectivity follows
from Lemma 4.6 as f restricts to the isomorphism P(g) → P Û(g). We conclude
that f is injective and thus it is an isomorphism by Lemma 2.9.                       

5. The Lazard correspondence for Lie R-algebras and Lie R-groups
Definition 5.1. Let R be a commutative ring. An R-group is a group G with a
map R × G → G : (r, g) 7→ g r satisfying for all r, s ∈ R, g, h ∈ G
   (1) g 1 = g,
   (2) g r+s = g r g s ,
   (3) g rs = (g r )s ,
   (4) hg r h−1 = (hgh−1 )r (where h−1 denotes the inverse of h).
A homomorphism of f : G → H of R-groups is a group homomorphism such that
moreover f (g r ) = f (g)r for all g ∈ G, r ∈ R.
   Note that R-groups were also defined in [41], but their definition has the extra
restriction that the Hall-Petresco formula should hold. However, we will impose
a similar condition for R-groups later on in the form of (G3). We can make the
following easy observations in an R-group G, for r ∈ R, g ∈ G:
     (1) g 0 = g 0 g 0 hence g 0 = 1,
     (2) 1 = g 0 = g r g −r hence g −r is the inverse of g r ,
     (3) for every n = 1 + . . . + 1 ∈ R, the element g n is necessarily the n-th power
         of g in G.
In particular, every group has a unique Z-group structure.
Proposition 5.2. Let G be a group and let Qk be as in Example 3.2 Then G is
Qk -group if and only if for every g ∈ G and every prime p ≤ k there exists a unique
h ∈ G such that hp = g. Moreover, any group has at most one possible Q-group
structure.
                                                                      1
Proof. Assume that G is a Qk -group and p ≤ k then clearly (g p )p = g. If h is
                                             1     1
any element such that hp = g, then h = (hp ) p = g p , which proves the uniqueness.
Conversely, assume that for every g and p ≤ k there exists a unique h such that
hp = g. Then in particular for every n whose prime divisors are at most k, we
                                                                   √
can find a unique h such that hn = g, we denote this element n g. The unique
                                                      q    √
Qk -group structure should necessarily be given by g r := r g q . One easily verifies
that G indeed becomes a Qk -group.                                                 
Definition 5.3. A filtered group is a group G together with a descending filtration
of normal subgroups G = G0 ⊇ G1 ⊇ ... such that [Gi , Gj ] ⊆ Gi+j for all i, j ≥ 1,
where [−, −] denotes the group theoretic commutator. A homomorphism of filtered
groups f : G → H is a group homomorphism such that f (Gi ) ⊆ Hi .
          LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE, SKEW BRACES AND POST-LIE RINGS                        13

                                    T
   A filtered group G is complete if Gi = {e} and it is complete with respect to
the topology generated by the base {gGi | g ∈ G, i ≥ 1}. A filtered group is G
connected if G0 = G1 .

Definition 5.4. An R-group is a filtered group G such that
  (G1) Gi is an Ri -group for every i ≥ 1,
  (G2) for any i ≥ 0, r ∈ Ri and g ∈ Gi , g r = g di (r) ,
  (G3) (gh)r Gi+1 = g r hr Gi+1 , for all i ≥ j ≥ 0, g ∈ Gi , h ∈ Gj , r ∈ Rj .
A homomorphism of R-groups f : G → H is a homomorphism of filtered groups
such that f : Gi → Hi is a Ri -group homomorphism for all i ≥ 0. The category of
complete connected R-group is denoted R Grc,c .

Example 5.5. Let G be a group and define G0 = G1 = G and Gi+1 = [G, Gi ] for
i ≥ 1. Then G has a unique Z-group structure.

Proposition 5.6. Let G be a filtered group. Then G is Q-group if and only if for
every i ≥ 1, every g ∈ Gi and every prime p ≤ i, there exists a unique element
h ∈ Gi such that hp = g.
   If moreover G is torsion, then G is a Q-group if and only if gcd(|g|, i) = 1 for
all i ≥ 1, g ∈ Gi , where |g| denotes the order of g. Moreover, every subgroup of
G is a sub R-group and the automorphisms of G as a Q-group coincide with the
automorphisms of G as a filtered group.

Proof. The first part follows directly from Proposition 5.2 and an easy verification
of (G3).
    Let g ∈ Gi , if |g| is coprime to p as then by Bezout’s theorem there exists some
r, s such that 1 = rp + s|g|, hence (g r )p = g and g r ∈ Gi . If hp = g for some other
h ∈ Gi , then since |h| is coprime to p, we find |g| = |hp | = |h| thus h = (hp )r = g r .
Conversely, if for some i ≥ 1, p ≤ i and g ∈ Gi , p divides |g|, then without loss of
generality |g| = p. If h ∈ Gi is such hp = g, then also (hg)p hence the uniqueness
is not satisfied.                                                                     
                                                                      P∞
   Let A be a complete R-algebra with R divisible. Then exp(a) := i=0 i!1 ai is a
                                                             P∞
well-defined element of 1+A1 for any a ∈ A1 . Also, log(a) := i=1 1i (−1)i+1 (a−1)i
is a well-defined element of A1 for any a ∈ 1 + A1 .
   For a complete Hopf R-algebra H an element g ∈ H is grouplike if ∆(g) = g ⊗g.ˆ
The set of grouplike elements of H is denoted G(H). Note that this immediately
implies that gS(g) = S(g)g = 1 hence G(H) is a group.

Theorem 5.7. Let R be divisible and H be a complete R-algebra, then exp and
log yield bijections between the sets 1 + Hi and Hi for all i ≥ 1. If moreover H
is a complete connected Hopf R-algebra then this bijection restricts to a bijection

Proposition 5.9. Let R be divisible and let H be a complete connected Hopf R-
algebra. Then G(H) is a complete R-group if we set G(H)i = G(H) ∩ (1 + Hi )
and g r = exp(r log(g)) for g ∈ G(H)i and r ∈ Ri . Moreover, exp(x + P(H)i ) =
exp(x) G(H)i , for all i ≥ 1 hence exp and log are homeomorphisms between P(H)
and G(H).
Proof. For simplicity let us denote G = G(H). Clearly 1 + Hi is closed under
multiplication, hence Gi is closed under multiplication. It is clear from the definition
that if g ∈ Gi , then also g r ∈ Gi for r ∈ Ri , so in particular g −1 ∈ Gi . One easily
sees that (G1) and (G2) hold.
   As exp(x + Hi ) ⊆ exp(x) + Hi and log(exp(x) + Hi ) ⊆ x + Hi for any x ∈ P(H),
we find indeed that exp(x + P(H)i ) = exp(x)Gi . We conclude that exp and log are
homeomorphisms between P(H) and G so in particular G is complete.
   The fact that [Gi , Gj ] ⊆ Gi+j follows from Lemma 5.8.
   We conclude by proving that (G3) holds. Let i ≥ j ≥ 0, g ∈ Gi , h ∈ Gj and
r ∈ Rj , because g and h commute in H/Hi+1 we find
          (gh)r + Hi+1 = exp(r log(g) + r log(h)) + Hi+1 = g r hr + Hi+1 .            
Lemma 5.10.S∞Let G be an R-group generated by X ⊆ G, then |G| ≤ max{|X|, α, ℵ0 }

Ai+1 = {br | b ∈ B, r ∈ Rdeg b }. If we let H be the union of the chain A0 ⊆ B0 ⊆
A1 ⊆ B1 ⊆ ..., then H is a sub R-group of G. Note that |Bi | ≤ max{|Ai |, ℵ0 }. Also,
           LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE, SKEW BRACES AND POST-LIE RINGS                          15


|Ai+1 | ≤ α|Bi |. In particular, |Ai | ≤ max{|X|, α, ℵ0 }, hence |H| ≤ max{|X|, α, ℵ0 }
and thus |G| ≤ max{|X|, α, ℵ0 }.                                                    

Proposition 5.11. The forgetful functor R Gr → Setf : G 7→ G has a left adjoint
F : Setf → R Gr.
Proof. By the adjoint functor theorem (see for example [7, Section 3]) it is sufficient
to prove that the category R Gr is complete, locally small and the solution set
condition is satisfied by the forgetful functor.                         Q
    Let (Gi )Q
             i∈I be a family
                          Qof R-groups. Then usual product of groups i∈I Gi , with
filtration ( i∈I Gi )k = i∈I (Gi )k and the R-group structure defined pointwise is
an R-group which clearly is a product in R Gr. Given two R-groups G and H and
homomorphisms φ, ψ : G → H, one easily verifies that E = {g ∈ G | φ(g) = ψ(g)}
is an R-subgroup of G, the injection map E → G is the equalizer of ψ and φ.
The two above facts combined prove that R Gr is a complete category. Since the
forgetful functor is faithful, R Gr is locally small.
    We now prove that the forgetful functor satisfies the solution set condition. Let
X be a filtered set and consider the class GX consisting of all pairs (G, f ) where
G is an R-group, f : X → G a homomorphism of filtered sets and f (X) generates
G as an R-group. Two pairs (G, f ), (H, g) ∈ GX are said to be isomorphic if there
exists an R-group isomorphism φ : G → H such that g = φf . Proving that the
forgetful functor satisfies the solution set condition amounts to proving that the
isomorphism classes of GX form a set. It follows from Lemma 5.10 that for any
(G, f ) ∈ GX , G has cardinality at most max{|X|, α, ℵ0 }. As for every set Y of a
given cardinality the cardinality of all possible group structures on Y is bounded
                  2
above by |Y ||Y | , the cardinality of all possible filtrations on Y is bounded above
by |N|2|Y | and for a given group structure and filtration on Y the number of R-
group structures is bounded above by |Y ||Y |α . We conclude that the class GX is
essentially small.                                                                   

   Let gLbe a Lie R-algebra. Its associated graded Lie R-algebra is the R-module
gr g := ∞  i=1 gi /gi+1 , with [x + gdeg(x)+1 , y + gdeg(y)+1 ] = [x, y] + gdeg(x)+deg(y)+1 .
One easily verifies that this is indeed a Lie R-algebra and that this construction is
functorial.
   Similarly, starting from G an R-group we can construct its associated graded Lie
R-algebra. First note that Gi /Gi+1 becomes an Ri -module by setting gGi+1 +
hGi+1 = ghGi+1 and r(gGi+1 ) = g r Gi+1         L,∞so it becomes an R-module as de-

ghg −1 h−1 Gi+j+1 . It is a classic result, that [−, −] is a Lie bracket, which is more-
over R-bilinear as for r ∈ Ri we have
            [rgGi+1 , hGj+1 ] = g r hg −r h−1 Gi+j+1 = g r (hg −1 h−1 )r Gi+j+1
                              = (ghg −1 h−1 )r Gi+j+1 = r[g, h]Gi+j+1 ,
since (ghg −1 h−1 )r (hgh−1 )r Gi+j+1 = g r Gi+j+i by (G3). Once again it is easily
verified that this construction is functorial.

Lemma 5.13. Let f : G → H be a homomorphism of complete R-groups, then
  (1) f is degree preserving if and only if gr f is injective,
  (2) f is a regular surjection if and only if gr f is surjective.
Proof. The first claim is easily seen to hold. Also, it is clear that if f is a regular
surjection, then gr f is surjective.
   Assume that f is such that gr f is surjective. We will show that f (Gi ) = Hi
for any i ≥ 1. Let h ∈ Hi . As gr f is surjective, there exists some g1 ∈ Gi such
that h−1 f (g1 ) ∈ Hi+1 . Subsequently, there also exists some g2 ∈ Gi+1 such that
h−1 f (g1 )f (g2 ) ∈ Gi+2 . We can continue this process in order to obtain
                                                                      Q      gj ∈ Gi+j
such that h−1 f (g1 · · · gj ) ∈ Hi+j . In particular, the limit g = ∞  i=1 j satisfies
                                                                            g
h−1 f (g). At last, note that Gi is closed hence g ∈ Gi .                            
   We denote the category of connected filtered sets by Setcon

Lemma 5.14. Let R be divisible. We have the following adjunctions of functors:
  (1) The functor P R[[−]] : Setcon
                                f   → R Liec,c is left adjoint to the forgetful
                   c,c     con
      functor R Lie → Setf .
  (2) The functor G R[[−]] : Setcon
                                 f  → R Grc,c is left adjoint to the forgetful
                   c,c     con
      functor R Gr → Setf .
Proof. The first claim follows directly from Lemma 2.7, Proposition 2.18 and The-
orem 4.7.
   Let X be a connected filtered set and let G = F    \ (X) be the completion of
the free R-group generated by X, which is easily seen to be the free complete
connected R-group generated by X. Then there exists a unique homomorphism
f : G → G R[[X]] mapping x ∈ X to exp(x). By the first part of the statement
we obtain a Lie R-algebra homomorphism u : P R[[X]] → gr G mapping x to
xGdeg(x)+1 , hence also a Lie R-algebra homomorphism gr u : gr P R[[X]] → gr G
mapping x + P(R[[X]])deg(x)+1 to xGdeg(x)+1 by the functoriality of gr. Now up
to the isomorphism gr P R[[X]] ∼= gr G R[[X]] in Proposition 5.12, we find that gr u
and gr f are mutually inverse hence f is an isomorphism by Lemma 5.13.            
Corollary 5.15. Let R be divisible and let X be filtered set, then P(R[[X]]), respec-
tively G(R[[X]]), is generated by X as a closed Lie R-algebra, respectively closed
R-group.
Proof. This follows directly from the freeness of P R[[X]] and G R[[X]].             
Corollary 5.16. Let R be divisible and let H be a complete connected Hopf R-
algebra. Consider {x, y} with filtration {x, y}1 = {x, y} and {x, y}i = ∅ for i > 1.

                            log(exp(a) exp(b)) = P (a, b),
for all a, b ∈ P(H).

           exp(log(a) + log(b)) = Q(a, b), exp([log(a), log(b)] = R(a, b),
for all a, b ∈ G(H).

Proof. This follows directly from Corollary 5.15.                                                               
Remark 5.17. It is well-known, see for example [14], that
                     1          1                           1

                     2         12                           24

known as the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula. Also

where in this case [a, b] = aba−1 b−1 and further factors involve iterated brackets of
order at least 5.

  Let H be a Hopf R-algebra and h ∈ H. We define adh : H → H : a 7→ ha − ah

Lemma 5.19. Let R be divisible and let H be a complete connected Hopf R-algebra.
Then exp(adx ) = conjexp(x) in EndR (H) for x ∈ P(H).
Proof. One easily verifies that φ : H → EndR (H) given by φh (y) = h(1) yS(h(2) )
is a well-defined homomorphism of R-algebras. For x a primitive element we now
find exp(adx ) = exp(φx ) = φexp(x) = conjexp(x) which proves the statement.  
Proposition 5.20. Let R be divisible and let H be a complete connected Hopf R-
algebra. Then there is a correspondence between closed sub Lie R-algebras of P(H)
and closed sub R-groups of G(H). This correspondence restricts to closed ideals of
P(H) and closed normal sub R-groups of G(H).
Proof. Consider the set X = {x, y} with filtration X1 = X, Xi = ∅ for i > 1.
For a, b ∈ P(H), consider the unique Hopf R-algebra homomorphism R[[X]] →
H mapping x 7→ a and y 7→ b. By Corollary 5.15 we find that exp maps the
closed sub Lie R-algebra generated by a, b to the closed sub R-group generated by
exp(a), exp(b). This proves the first part of the statement.
   The second part now follows directly by Lemma 5.19.                          
   Let g be a complete connected Lie R-algebra. Then G Û(g) = exp(g) is a
complete R-group by Proposition 5.9. We transfer the R-group structure onto g
through exp and log, and denote this new group operation by BCH, so BCH(g, h) =
log(exp(g) exp(h)) and g r = rg. By Corollary 5.16 we find that this construction is
functorial and thus we obtain a functor Laz : R Liec,c → R Grc,c .
Theorem 5.21. Let R be divisible. The functors Laz : R Liec,c → R Grc,c and
Laz−1 : R Grc,c → R Liec,c yield an equivalence of categories, where Laz(g) = (g, ·)
with
               x · y = BCH(x, y), rx = xr for x, y ∈ g, r ∈ Rdeg(x) ,
and Laz(G) = (G, +, [−, −]) with
         x + y = Q(x, y), [x, y] = R(x, y), xr = rx for x, y ∈ G, r ∈ Rdeg(x) .
18                                   S. TRAPPENIERS


Proof. From the previous discussion we know that Laz is a well-defined functor.
   If G is complete connected R-group such that G = Laz(g) for some complete
connected Lie R-algebra g, then by Corollary 5.16 it follows that Laz−1 (G) = g.
We show that every complete connected R-group G is isomorphic to Laz(g) for
some complete connected Lie R-algebra g. By Lemma 5.14 there exists a regu-
lar surjection Laz(P R[[G]]) → G. Hence G ∼  = Laz(P R[[G]])/N for some nor-
mal sub R-group N of Laz(P R[[G]]). However, by Proposition 5.20 we find that
Laz(P R[[G]])/N = Laz(P R[[G]]/N ). At last, note that also Laz−1 is functo-
rial.                                                                           

                               6. Post-Lie R-algebras
Lemma 6.1. Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie ring. Then (a, ⊲) is L-nilpotent if and only if
(a, ⊲) is left nilpotent and a is a nilpotent Lie ring.
Proof. From the definition of Li (a) it is clear that if (a, ⊲) is L-nilpotent then it is
left nilpotent and a is a nilpotent Lie ring.
   Conversely, assume that (a, ⊲) is left nilpotent and a is a nilpotent Lie ring. Let
a = a1 ⊇ ... ⊇ ad = 0 denote the lower central series of a and let c be such that
ac+1 = 1. If we assume that Li (a) ⊆ ak for some i, k ≥ 1, then [Li (a), a] ⊆ ak+1
hence Li+1 (a) ⊆ (a ⊲ Li (a)) + ak+1 . In particular, Li+c (a) ⊆ ac+1 + ak+1 = ak+1 .
We now conclude by induction that Lkc+1 (a) = ad = 1.                                  

Definition 6.2. A post-Lie R-algebra is a Lie R-algebra a together with a map
⊲ : a × a → a such that
     (P 1) La ∈ EndR (a) for all a ∈ a, where La : a → a : b 7→ a ⊲ b,
     (P 2) (a + b) ⊲ c = a ⊲ c + b ⊲ c for all a, b, c ∈ a,
     (P 3) Lra = rLa for all a ∈ ai , r ∈ Ri whenever La ∈ EndR (M )i ,
     (P 4) ⊲ satisfies (1.1) and (1.2).
If a is abelian, then (a, ⊲) is a pre-Lie R-algebra.
   A homomorphism of post-Lie R-algebras f : (a, ⊲) → (b, ⊲) is a map that respects
the Lie R-algebra structure and moreover f (a ⊲ b) = f (a) ⊲ f (b) for all a, b ∈ a.
   A sub Lie R-algebra I of (a, ⊲) is
      (1) a left ideal if x ⊲ y ∈ I for all x ∈ a, y ∈ I,
      (2) a strong left ideal if it is a left ideal and it is an ideal of a,
      (3) an ideal if it is a strong left ideal and moreover I is an ideal of a◦ .
Example 6.3. Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie R-algebra. Then (a, ⊲) is a post-Lie R-
algebra for the filtration a0 = a, ai = Li (a) for i ≥ 1.
Example 6.4. Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie R-algebra, then
                        Fix(a) := {a ∈ a | b ⊲ a = 0 for all b ∈ a},
is a left ideal and
                    Soc(a) := {a ∈ a | a ⊲ b = [a, b] = 0 for all b ∈ a}
is an ideal. For the latter statement, note that for a ∈ Soc(a) and b, c ∈ a, it follows
from (1.1) that 0 = b ⊲ [a, c] = [b ⊲ a, c] and from (1.2) that 0 = [a, b] ⊲ c = −(b ⊲ a) ⊲ c
hence b ⊲ a ∈ Soc(a). As {b, a} = b ⊲ a, Soc(a) is an ideal.
Definition 6.5. Let g be a Lie R-algebra. A map δ ∈ EndR (g) is a derivation
if δ([x, y]) = [δ(x), y] + [x, δ(y)] for all x, y ∈ g. We define Der(g) as the set of
all derivations of g, which are easily seen to form a sub Lie R-algebra of EndR (g)
under the usual commutator Lie bracket.
          LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE, SKEW BRACES AND POST-LIE RINGS                         19


Lemma 6.6. Let g be a Lie R-algebra, then the direct product of R-modules
aff(g) := g ⊕ Der(g) together with Lie bracket
                     [(g, δ), (h, χ)] = ([g, h] + δ(h) − χ(g), [δ, χ]),
is a Lie R-algebra. We denote the projection onto g by prg .
Definition 6.7. Let a be a Lie R-algebra, a sub Lie R-algebra g of aff(a) is t-
surjective, respectively t-bijective if pra : g → a is surjective, respectively bijective.
Proposition 6.8. Let a be a Lie R-algebra. Then there is a bijective correspon-
dence between maps ⊲ : a × a → a making (a, ⊲) into a post-Lie R-algebra and
t-bijective sub Lie R-algebras of aff(a).
Proof. Let a be a Lie R-algebra and ⊲ : a × a → a any map. The maps La : a →
a : b 7→ a ⊲ b, for a ∈ a, are contained in EndR (a) if and only if (P 1) holds. The
La are derivations of a if and only if (1.1) holds. Suppose that all of the previous
assumptions are satisfied and consider g = {(x, Lx ) | x ∈ a} ∈ aff(a). Conditions
(P 2) and (P 3) are satisfied precisely if g is a sub R-module of aff(a). We see that
g is a sub Lie R-algebra if L[x,y]+x⊲y−y⊲x = [Lx , Ly ] which is equivalent to (1.2).
This proves the correspondence.                                                    

Corollary 6.9. Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie R-algebra. We obtain a new Lie R-algebra
structure a◦ on a with filtration a◦i = {a ∈ ai | La ∈ Der(a)i } and Lie bracket
                             {a, b} := [a, b] + a ⊲ b − b ⊲ a.
Remark 6.10. Note that the at first somewhat artificial definition of a post-Lie
R-algebra becomes more natural when we remark that (P 1) − (P 3) state precisely
that a◦ × a → a is an R-bilinear map.
Proof. Let g be the associated t-bijective sub Lie R-algebra of aff(a) as in Propo-
sition 6.8. The statement follows by transferring the Lie R-algebra structure of g
onto a through the bijection pra : g → a.                                        

Definition 6.11. Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie R-algebra, then (a, ⊲) is
    (1) connected if both a and a◦ are connected Lie R-algebras,
    (2) complete if both a and a◦ are complete Lie R-algebras.
The category of complete connected post-Lie R-algebras is denoted R PLAc,c .
Example 6.12. Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie R-algebra, then the associated post-Lie
R-algebra as in Example 6.3 is connected. If (a, ⊲) is L-nilpotent, it is complete.
    Let F be a field of characteristic 0 and (a, ⊲) be a finite dimensional pre-Lie F-
algebra. Then the classical definition of completeness, as coined in [19], is that for
every a ∈ a, the map ra : a → a : b 7→ b + a ⊲ b is a bijection. However, if a◦ is
nilpotent, then [32, Proposition 2] states that all maps ra are bijective if and only
if left multiplication maps La are nilpotent. By Engel’s theorem, this is equivalent
with the existence of some n such that La1 · · · Lan = 0 for all a1 , . . . , an ∈ a. It
follows that this notion of completeness coincides with what we call left nilpotency.
Therefore, a pre-Lie F-algebra (a, ⊲) with a◦ nilpotent is complete if and only if
its associated pre-Lie F -algebra (as in Example 6.3) is complete. Note that the
condition that all La are nilpotent also appears in [10, Theorem 3.1].
Theorem 6.13. Let (a, ⊲) be an L-nilpotent post-Lie ring of class k. Then a◦ is
nilpotent of class at most k and the k-th term in the lower central series of a◦ is
contained in Ann(a), where Ann(a) := Soc(a) ∩ Fix(a).
20                                 S. TRAPPENIERS


Proof. Let (a, ⊲) be L-nilpotent of class k and consider it as a post-Lie Z-algebra.
Then a◦k+1 ⊆ ak+1 = 0, hence in particular a◦ is nilpotent of class at most k.
Also, since a◦k = ak ∩ {a ∈ a | La ∈ EndR (a)k } but EndR (a)k = 0 and clearly
ak ∈ Z(a) ∩ Fix(a), the statement follows.                                        

                                 7. Skew R-braces
   We start by noting that one can prove Lemma 1.2 using almost the same proof
as for Lemma 6.1.
Definition 7.1. A skew R-brace is an R-group (A, ·) with an additional group
structure (A, ◦) such that
   (S1) a ◦ (b · c) = (a ◦ b) · a−1 · (a ◦ c),
   (S2) a ∗ b ∈ Ai+1 and λa (br ) = λa (b)r for a ∈ A, b ∈ Ai , r ∈ Ri ,
where we define a ∗ b = a−1 · (a ◦ b) · b−1 and λa (b) = a−1 · (a ◦ b). An R-brace is an
skew R-brace with an abelian additive group. A homomorphism of skew R-braces
f : (A, ·, ◦) → (B, ·, ◦) is a map such that f : (A, ·) → (B, ·) is a homomorphism of
R-groups and f : (A, ◦) → (B, ◦) is a group homomorphism.
   A sub R-group I of (A, ·) is
     (1) a sub skew R-brace if I is a subgroup of (A, ◦),
     (2) a left ideal if λa (b) ∈ I for all a ∈ A, b ∈ I,
     (3) a strong left ideal if I is a left ideal and also a normal subgroup of (A, ·),
     (4) an ideal if I is a strong left ideal and also a normal subgroup of (A, ◦).
Example 7.2. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew brace, then the filtration A0 = A, Ai = Li (A)
for i ≥ 1 makes it into a skew Z-brace.
Example 7.3. Let (A, ·, ◦) be an R-brace, see [16, Definition 2], and consider the
associated Z-brace as in Example 7.2. Then Li (A) is a sub R-modules of A for every
i ≥ 1, since a ∗ (rb) = r(a ∗ b) for r ∈ R, a, b ∈ A. In this way the obtained Z-brace
has a natural R-brace structure. Conversely, any R-brace becomes an R-brace if
we simply forget the filtration.
Definition 7.4. For G an R-group, we define Aut(G) as all R-group automor-
phisms of G. We define a filtration Aut(G)i by
                  Aut(G)i = {f | f (g)g −1 ∈ Gi+j , for all g ∈ Gj }
Remark 7.5. In Definition 7.1 it follows from (S1) that λa (b · c) = λa (b) · λa (c),
hence (S2) can be rephrased as λa ∈ Aut(A, ·)1 .
Lemma 7.6. Let G be an R-group, then Hol(G) := G ⋊ Aut(G) with Hol(G)i =
Gi ⋊ Aut(G)i is a filtered group. We denote the projection onto G by prG .
Definition 7.7. Let G be an R-group. A subgroup H ≤ Hol(G) is transitive,
respectively regular, if prG : H → G is surjective, respectively bijective.
Remark 7.8. Note that if we consider the natural action of Hol(G) on G, i.e. (g, λ) ·
h = gλ(h), then transitive subgroups of Hol(G) are precisely the ones such that the
associated action is transitive.
Proposition 7.9. Let (A, ·) be an R-group. There is a bijective correspondence
between group structures (A, ◦) making (A, ·, ◦) into a skew R-brace and regular
subgroups of Hol(A, ·).
Proof. We only sketch the proof, as this is a slight variation of [18, Theorem 4.2].
Let (A, ◦) be a group operation such that (A, ·, ◦) is a skew R-brace. Define G =
{(a, λa ) | a ∈ A} ≤ Hol(A), then G is a regular subgroup of Hol(A). Conversely,
          LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE, SKEW BRACES AND POST-LIE RINGS                   21


if G is a regular subgroup of Hol(A), we transfer the group structure of G onto A
with the help of the bijection prA : G → A and we denote this new group operation
by ◦. Then (A, ·, ◦) becomes a skew R-brace.                                    

Corollary 7.10. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew R-brace. Then (A, ◦) with the filtration
(A, ◦)i = Ai ∩ {a ∈ A | λa ∈ Aut(A)i } is a filtered group.
Proof. Let G be the associated regular subgroup of Hom(A, ·) as in Proposition 7.9
with filtration coming from Hom(A, ·). Transferring the filtration of G onto (A, ◦)
through the isomorphism (A, ◦) → G : a 7→ (a, λa ) now yields the statement.     

Definition 7.11. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew R-brace, then (A, ·, ◦) is
   (1) connected if both (A, ·) and (A, ◦) are connected filtered groups,
   (2) complete if both (A, ·) and (A, ◦) are complete filtered groups.
Example 7.12. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew brace, then the associated skew Z-brace as
in Example 7.2 is connected. If (A, ·, ◦) is L-nilpotent, it is complete. The same
applies for the R-braces as obtained in Example 7.3.
  The proof of Theorem 1.3 similar to the proof of Theorem 6.13.

   8. A Lazard correspondence for post-Lie R-algebras and skew
                             R-braces
Definition 8.1. For g a Lie R-algebra we define Aut(g) as the set of all Lie R-
algebra automorphisms with filtration Aut(g)i = Aut(g) ∩ (id + EndR (g)i ).
Definition 8.2. For a filtered set X we define X + as the connected filtered subset
consisting of all elements of X1 . The same notation is used also for R-modules and
R-groups.
Lemma 8.3. Let R be divisible and let g be a complete Lie R-algebra. Then
Aut(g)i = exp(Der(g)i ) for i ≥ 1. In particular, the group Aut(g)+ has a canon-
ical R-group structure such that exp : Laz(Der(g)+ ) → Aut(g)+ is an R-group
isomorphism.
Proof. Let X = {x} with the filtration X1 = X, X2 = ∅ and let R[[x]] := R[[X]].
For any R-module homomorphism φ : R[[x]] → EndR (g) the set
                S = {h ∈ R[[x]] | [−, −](φh(1) ⊗ φh(2) ) = φh [−, −]}
is a closed sub R-algebra of R[[x]]. As {x} and {exp(x)} generate R[[x]] as a
closed sub R-algebra, we find that φx ∈ Der(g)i if and only if φexp(x) ∈ Aut(g)i .
For any element f of EndR (g)1 there exists a unique R-algebra homomorphism
R[[x]] → EndR (H) mapping x to f , so for every element g ∈ 1 + EndR (g)1 there
exists a unique R-algebra homomorphism R[[x]] → EndR (H) mapping exp(x) to
g. This implies for any i ≥ 1 that δ ∈ Der(g)i if and only if exp(δ) ∈ Aut(g)i . 

Lemma 8.4. Let R be divisible and let g be a complete Lie R-algebra. Then
Aut(Û(g))i = exp(Der(Û (g))i ) for i ≥ 1. In particular, the group Aut(Û(g))+ has
a canonical R-group structure such that exp : Laz(Der(Û(g))+ ) → Aut(Û (g))+ is
an R-group isomorphism.
Proof. The proof is analogous to the proof of Lemma 8.3.                          

Lemma 8.5. Let R be divisible and let g be a complete connected Lie R-algebra,
then Aut(g) = Aut(Laz(g)).
22                                         S. TRAPPENIERS


Proof. We know by Theorem 5.21 that automorphisms of g and G coincide. It
remains to verify that the filtrations coincide. Denote H = Û(g), let x, y ∈ P(H)
and denote d = deg(x + y). Then [x, y] + Hd+1 = [x, y] − [x + y, y] + Hd+1 = Hd+1 ,
hence x + y + Hd+1 = BCH(x, y) + Hd+1 by Remark 5.17. In particular, for
δ ∈ Der(g)+ we find deg(BCH(exp(δ)(x), −x)) = deg(exp(δ)(x) − x), thus the
degree of exp(δ) in Aut(Laz(g)) equals the degree of exp(δ) − id in EndR (g), which
is easily seen to equal the degree of δ in EndR (g) (or equivalently in Der(g)+ ). 
Proposition 8.6. Let R be divisible and let a be a complete connected Lie R-
algebra, then
             γ : Laz(aff(a)+ ) → Hol(Laz(a))+ : (a, δ) 7→ (V (a, δ), exp(δ)),
with V (a, δ) = pra (BCH((a, δ), (0, −δ))) is an isomorphism of filtered groups.
   In particular, Hol(Laz(a))+ has an R-group structure such that f is an isomor-
phism of R-groups.
Proof. We will work inside of H = Û(aff(a)+ ) and we identify a and Der(a)+
with their corresponding sub Lie R-algebras of aff(a)+ = P(H). Note that by
Lemma 5.19 and Lemma 8.3 the map
      f : exp(a) exp(Der(a)+ ) → Hol(Laz(a))+ : exp(a, 0) exp(0, δ) 7→ (a, exp(δ))
is a filtered group isomorphism.
   Let (a, δ) ∈ aff(a)+ , then log(exp(a, δ) exp(0, −δ)) + aff(a)+ = aff(a)+ , hence
exp(a, δ) exp(0, −δ) ∈ exp(a). We conclude that
           exp(a, δ) = (exp(a, δ) exp(0, −δ)) exp(0, δ) ∈ exp(a) exp(Der(a)+ ),
meaning that
     Laz(aff(a)+ ) → exp(a) exp(Der(a)+ ) : (a, δ) 7→ (exp(a, δ) exp(0, −δ)) exp(0, δ),
is an R-group isomorphism. Composing this isomorphism with f we find indeed
that γ is an isomorphism of groups.                                       
Remark 8.7. We can explicitly write γ −1 (a, λ) = (U (a, λ), log(λ)), where U (a, λ) =
pra (P ((a, λ), (0, λ−1 ))) with P as in Corollary 5.16. The proof for this is analogous
to the one of Proposition 8.6.
Definition 8.8. If R is a divisible sequence of rings then a skew R-brace (A, ·, ◦)
is strict if the corresponding regular subgroup of Hol(A, ·) is a sub R-group, with
the R-group structure of Hol(A, ·) as in Proposition 8.6.
     The following example shows that there exist R-braces that are not strict.
Example 8.9. Let R be a commutative ring of characteristic different from 2 and
f : (R, +) → (R, +) a group endomorphism. Then the sequence R = R → R →
R → 0 → ... is divisible. On M = R ⊕ R we consider the filtration M0 = M1 = M ,
M2 = R ⊕ 0, Mi = 0 for i ≥ 3, with the canonical R-module structure coming from
the R-module structure. On M we define
                     (x1 , y1 ) ◦ (x2 , y2 ) = (x1 + x2 + f (y1 )y2 , y1 + y2 ),
which is easily verified to be a group structure. Also
 (x1 , y1 )◦((x2 , y2 ) + (x3 , y3 )) = (x1 + x2 + x3 + f (y1 )(y2 + y3 ), y1 + y2 + y3 )
             = (x1 + x2 + f (y1 )y2 , y1 + y2 ) − (x1 , y1 ) + (x1 + x3 + f (y1 )y3 , y1 + y3 )
             = (x1 , y1 ) ◦ (x2 , y2 ) − (x1 , y1 ) + (x1 , y1 ) ◦ (x3 , y3 ),
and λ(x1 ,y1 ) (x2 , y2 ) = (x2 + f (y1 )y2 , y2 ), hence λ(x,y) ∈ Aut+ (M ) meaning that
(M, +, ◦) is an R-brace. We find log(λ(a,b) )(x, y) = (f (b)y, 0) and thus λr(a,b) is
             LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE, SKEW BRACES AND POST-LIE RINGS                        23


given by (x, y) 7→ (x + rf (b)y, y). Hence, λr(a,b) = λ(c,d) if and only if rf (b) = f (d),
hence λ(M ) is a sub R-group of Aut(M )+ if and only if f (R) is a left ideal of
R. Note that λ(M ) being a sub R-group of Aut(M )+ is a necessary condition for
(M, +, ◦) to be strict.
Proposition 8.10. Let R be divisible, let a be a complete connected Lie R-algebra
and set A = Laz(a). Then γ yields a bijective correspondence between closed sub
Lie R-algebras g of aff(a)+ and closed sub R-groups G of Hol(A)+ . Moreover,
pra : g → a is injective, respectively surjective, if and only if prA : γ(g) → A is
injective, respectively surjective.
Proof. The first part follows directly from Proposition 5.20 and Proposition 8.6.
    Assume that g is a closed Lie R-algebra of aff(a) such that pra : g → a is
not injective. As this map is R-linear, this means that there exists some non-zero
element δ ∈ g∩Der+ (a). But then clearly V (δ) = BCH(δ, −δ) = 0 = V (0), meaning
that V is not injective on g and thus prA : γ(g) → A is not injective.
    Conversely, assume that there exist (a, λ), (a, λ′ ) ∈ γ(g) with λ 6= λ′ . Then
(a, λ)−1 (a, λ′ ) = (0, λ−1 λ′ ) ∈ f (g). Hence there exists some (b, δ) ∈ aff(a) with
δ 6= 0 such that V (b, δ) = 0 hence b = 0.
    Assume that pra : g → a is surjective. We claim that prA γ = V : g → a is
surjective. Since prA and γ are continuous, the set V (g) is closed in a. Assume that
there exists some a ∈ A\prA γ(g), then there exists a d such that V (g)∩(a+ad ) 6= ∅
but V (g)∩(a+ad+1) = ∅. Let (b, δ) ∈ g such that V (b, δ) ∈ a+ad and let (b′ , δ ′ ) ∈ g
such that b′ = BCH(−V (b, δ), a). Since b′ ∈ ad , we have
(8.1)            b′ + ad+1 = V (b′ , δ ′ ) + ad+1 = exp(δ)(V (b′ , δ ′ )) + ad+1 .
Hence
        V (BCH((b, δ), (b′ , δ ′ ))) + ad+1 = BCH(V (b, δ), exp(δ)V (b′ , δ ′ )) + ad+1
                                          = BCH(V (b, δ), BCH(−V (b, δ), a)) + ai+1
                                          = a + ad+1 ,
where the first equality follows from the fact that γ is a group homomorphism. We
find BCH(−V (BCH((b, δ), (b′ , δ ′ ))), a) ∈ a + ad+1 , which is a contradiction.
   Conversely, assume that V (g) = a. Clearly pra (g) is closed in a because pra is
continuous. Assume that there exists some a ∈ a \ pra (g) and let d be such that
pra (g) ∩ (a + ad ) 6= ∅ but pra (g) ∩ (a + ad+1 ) = ∅. Choose (b, δ) ∈ g such that
b ∈ ad and choose (b′ , δ ′ ) ∈ g such that V (b′ , δ ′ ) = b − a. Using (8.1) we find
                    pra (h + h′ ) + ad+1 = b + V (h′ ) + ad+1 = a + ad+1 ,
hence pra (h + h′ ) ∈ a + ad+1 , which is a contradiction.                                
Remark 8.11. Transitive subgroups of the holomorph of a finite group play an
essential role in the theory of Hopf–Galois structures, see for example [13, 38, 23].
Although in general Hol+ (A) is a strict subgroup of Hol(A) one can prove that if
A is a p-group then there exists a finite filtration of A such that A is connected
and Hol(A)+ is a Sylow p-subgroup of Hol(A). If |A| = pk for k < p, then such a
filtration has length at most p so we can see A as a Z/p^  k Z-group. Hence in such

a case, we can classify all regular p-groups of Hol(A) by classifying the t-surjective
sub Lie rings of aff(Laz−1 (A)).
Definition 8.12. Let R be divisible and let (A, ·, ◦) be a complete connected skew
R-brace. Then (A, ·, ◦) is strict if it associated regular subgroup G of Hol(A, ·)+ is
a sub R-group, with the R-group structure as in Proposition 8.6, in this case we
transfer the R-group structure of G onto (A, ◦) through their canonical bijection. A
24                                  S. TRAPPENIERS


sub skew R-brace of (A, ·, ◦) is strict if it is a sub R-group of (A, ◦). The category
of strict complete connected skew R-braces is denoted R SBc,c,s .
Lemma 8.13. Let R be divisible and let (A, ·, ◦) be a strict complete connected
skew R-brace. Then every left ideal is a strict sub skew R-brace.
Proof. Let I be a left ideal of (A, ·, ◦). Since a ◦ b = a · λa (b), it is always true that
a left ideal is a sub skew R-brace. It remains to show that it is strict, which is
equivalent to I ′ = {(x, λx ) | x ∈ I} being a sub R-group of Hol(A, ·)+ . However,
I ′ = G ∩ (I ⋊ Aut(A, ·)+ ) where G is the associated regular subgroup of Hol(A, ·)+ .
By assumption, G is a sub R-group. It is easily verified that γ −1 (I ⋊ Aut(A, ·)+ ) =
I ⊕ Der(a)+ ≤ aff(a)+ with a = Laz(A, ·). Since I ⊕ Der(a)+ is a closed sub R-
algebra of aff(a)+ , we find that I ⋊ Aut(A, ·)+ is a sub R-group of Hol(A, ·). We
conclude that I ′ is an intersection of two sub R-groups, hence it is a sub R-group
itself.                                                                                  

Proposition 8.14. Let R be divisible and let (a, ⊲) be a complete connected post-Lie
R-algebra. Then
                          W : a → a : a 7→ V (a, La ),
is a bijective map and S(a, ⊲) = (a, ·, ◦) with (a, ·) = Laz(a), a◦b = a·exp(LΩ(a) )(b)
is a strict complete connected skew R-brace, where Ω := W −1 . Moreover, W :
Laz(a◦ ) → (a, ◦) is an R-group isomorphism.
Proof. Let (a, ⊲) be a complete connected post-Lie R-algebra and let g be the
regular sub Lie R-algebra of aff(a)+ associated to (a, ⊲). Then W is a bijection
since it is the composition of the bijections a → g : a 7→ (a, La ) and V : g → a,
recall that the latter is a bijection by Proposition 5.20.
   By Proposition 5.20 we find that γ(g) is a closed regular sub R-group of Hol(Laz(a))+ ,
thus we obtain a strict complete connected skew R-brace (a, ·, ◦) where (a, ·) =
Laz(a). Also a ◦ b = a · λa (b) where λa ∈ Aut(a) is uniquely determined by
(a, λa ) ∈ γ(g). Since γ(a) = {(W (a), exp(La )) | a ∈ a} we find λa = exp(LΩ(a) ).
   Also, W : Laz(a◦ ) → (a, ◦) is a group isomorphism because it is the composition
of the group homomorphisms Laz(a◦ ) → Laz(g) : a 7→ (a, La ), γ : Laz(g) → γ(g)
and pra : γ(g) → (a, ◦).                                                            

Remark 8.15. With the help of the explicit formula in Remark 5.17 find that
              1         1          1         1
 W (a) = a + La (a) + L2a (a) + [a, La (a)] + (La ([a, La (a)]) + L3a (a)) + ...
              2         6          12        24
where further terms are of order at least 5.
   We now explain how the above construction is related to the formal integration
as described by Bai, Guo, Sheng and Tang in [5]. Let F be a field of characteristic
0. Then Bai, Guo, Sheng and Tang proved that to any connected complete post-Lie
F-algebra (a, ⊲) one can associate a skew brace (a, ·, ◦) where
                     a · b = BCH(a, b), a ◦ b = a · exp(LΩ′ (a) )(b).
We first note that in our terminology their notion of a connected complete post-
Lie F-algebra is a connected complete post-Lie F-algebra (a, ⊲) such that moreover
ai ⊲ aj ⊆ ai+j , or equivalently, such that the filtrations on a and a◦ coincide. This
is indeed a more restrictive notion, as for example if ai = 0 for some i, then ai−1 is
contained in the socle hence Soc(a, ⊲) 6= 0. In [17, Section 3] an example is given
of a left-nilpotent pre-Lie R-algebra with trivial socle, so its associated pre-Lie R-
algebra, as in Example 6.3, is complete and connected in our sense but not in the
sense of [5].
          LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE, SKEW BRACES AND POST-LIE RINGS                     25


   We quickly recall their construction: starting from a complete post-Lie F-algebra
(a, ⊲) such that a◦i = ai for all i ≥ 0 and consider the universal enveloping algebra
U(a). On U(a) we define a new multiplication ∗ which for a ∈ a, b ∈ U (a) is given
by a ∗ b = ab + δa (b), where δa is the unique derivation of U(a) with δa (z) = a ⊲ z
for z ∈ a. In this way, (U (a), ∗) now becomes an F-algebra. This operation is
then extended to the completion Û(a) and (Û(a), ∗) filtration is thus a complete
F-algebra. For a ∈ a, we define Ω′ (a) = log∗ exp(a), where the exponential map
with respect to the usual multiplication in Û(a) is first applied, followed by the
logaritmic map in (Û(a), ∗).
   We prove that W (a) = log exp∗ (a), which implies that Ω = Ω′ and thus that
our construction coincides with the one in [5]. Consider the two F-algebra homo-
morphisms s, t : Û(a◦ ) → Û(aff(a)) given by s(a) = (a, La ) and t(a) = (0, La ). We
define
                     φ : Û(a◦ ) → Û(aff(a)) : a 7→ s(a(1 ))t(S(a(2) )).
Then φ(g) ∈ Û(a) ⊆ Û (aff(a)) for any grouplike element g ∈ G Û(a◦ ), hence the
image of φ is contained in U(a◦ ) since the grouplike elements span Û(a◦ ). Note
that for a ∈ a◦ , b ∈ Û(a◦ ),
                     φ(ab) = φ(a(1) )t(a(2) )(φ(b)) = φ(a) ∗ φ(b).
Hence
                   exp∗ φ(a) = φ exp(a) = exp(a, La ) exp(0, La )−1
thus log exp∗ (a) = W (a).
   In the pre-Lie case we have a more explicit description of W which coincides
with the one in [2] and [36].

Proposition 8.17. Let R be divisible and let (A, ·, ◦) be a strict complete connected
skew R-brace. Then
                             Ω : A 7→ A : a 7→ U (a, λa ),
is a bijection and L(A, ·, ◦) = (Laz−1 (A, ·), ⊲) with a ⊲ b = log(λW (a) )(b), is a

Theorem 8.19. Let R be divisible, then
             S : R PLAc,c → R SBc,c,s and L : R SBc,c,s → R PLAc,c ,
are mutually inverse functors. The map Ω associated to a complete connected post-
Lie R-algebra (a, ⊲) coincides with the map Ω associated to S(a, ⊲).
   Closed sub post-Lie R-algebras of (a, ⊲) and closed strict sub skew R-braces of
S(a, ⊲) coincide and moreover, closed left ideals, closed strong left ideals and closed
ideals of (a, ⊲) and S(a, ⊲) coincide.
          LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE, SKEW BRACES AND POST-LIE RINGS                        27


Proof. It is clear that S and L are mutually inverse constructions and that their
associated maps Ω coincide. We prove the functoriality of S, the proof for L is
analogous.
   Let f : (a, ⊲) → (b, ⊲) be a homomorphism of complete connected post-Lie R-
algebras and set (a, ·, ◦) = S(a, ⊲) and (b, ·, ◦) = S(b, ⊲). Then by Theorem 5.21
f : (a, ·) → (b, ·) is an R-group homomorphism. As W is an isomorphism between
Laz(a◦ ) and (a, ◦), it is sufficient to proof f W = W f in order to conclude that f :
(a, ◦) → (b, ◦) is a group homomorphism. Note that f ′ (a, La ) = (f (a), Lf (a) ) yields
a homomorphism between the closed sub Lie R-algebras a ⊕ {La | a ∈ a} ≤ aff(a)+
and b ⊕ {Lb | b ∈ b} ≤ aff(b)+ . In particular, we find that
                     f W (a) = f pra BCH((a, La )(0, −La ))
                             = prb f ′ BCH((a, La )(0, −La ))
                             = prb BCH((f (a), Lf (a) (0, −Lf (a) ))
                             = W f (a).
   The equivalence of closed sub post-Lie R-algebras and closed strict sub skew
R-braces is a direct corollary of Theorem 8.19. In particular, note that for b a
closed sub post-Lie R-algebra of (a, ⊲) this implies that on the set b, the map Wb
belonging to (b, ⊲) coincides with the map W belonging to (a, ⊲), so in particular
W (b) = b.
   Clearly the closed sub Lie R-algebras of a invariant under {Lx | x ∈ a} and
{exp(Lx ) | x ∈ a} coincide, which yields the equivalence of closed left ideals. Taking
into account Proposition 8.10, the equivalence of closed strong left ideals follows.
   Let b be a strong left ideal of (a, ⊲). As W : Laz(a◦ ) → (A, ◦) is a group
isomorphism, we find that b is an ideal of a◦ if and only if W (b) is a normal sub
R-group of (A, ◦). If we recall that W (b) = b, the equivalence of ideals of (a, ⊲)
and S(a, ⊲) follows.                                                                 
Remark 8.20. Recall that a skew brace (A, +, ◦) is square-free if a ∗ a for all a ∈ A.
Similarly, we say that a post-Lie ring (a, ⊲) is square-free if a ⊲ a = 0 for all a ∈ a.
Note that the property of being square-free is preserved by the functors S and L and
in particular, W = Ω = id in this case. Therefore these classes behave particularly
well and eliminate most of the computations involved.
Example 8.21. Let R be a divisible sequence and let A be a connected complete
R-algebra. Then A is a pre-Lie algebra for a ⊲ b = ab and it is well-known that the
associated group of flows is given by a ◦ b = a + ab + b. We can verify this directly:
clearly W (a) = exp(a) − 1, hence Ω(a) = log(1 + a), where we for simplicity we
work in the Dorroh extension R0 ⊕ A. We now find
                     a ◦ b = a + exp(Llog(1+a) )(b) = a + ab + b.
Conversely, just working in (A, +, ◦) we recover the original multiplication as
        a ⊲ b = log(λW (a) )(b) = log(L1+W (a) )(b) = a + log(Lexp(a) )(b) = ab.
Recall that this is precisely the well-known correspondence between two-sided braces
and Jacobson radical rings [30].
  The following result extends [37, Proposition 15, Lemma 17].
Proposition 8.22. Let R be divisible, let (A, ·, ◦) be a complete connected skew
R-brace and let n be an integer, then {an | a ∈ A} = {a◦n | a ∈ A} and {a ∈ A |
an = 1} = {a ∈ A | a◦n = 1} and these sets are closed ideals of (A, ·, ◦).
Proof. We prove the statement for the first set, the second part is analogous. Let
(a, ⊲) be the complete post-Lie R-algebra such that (A, ·, ◦) = S(a, ⊲). Then na is a
28                                  S. TRAPPENIERS


closed ideal of (a, ⊲), hence it is also a closed ideal of (A, ·, ◦) by Theorem 8.19. Now
as (A, ·) = Laz(a), we find na = {an | a ∈ A}. Also, as W : Laz(a◦ ) → (A, ◦) is
an R-group isomorphism we find W (na) = {a◦n | a ∈ A}, but as W maps any sub
post-Lie R-algebra to itself, we conclude that {an | a ∈ A} = {a◦n | a ∈ A}.            
Proposition 8.23. Let R be divisible and let (a, ⊲) be a complete connected post-Lie
R-algebra. Then Fix(a, ⊲) = Fix(S(a, ⊲)), Soc(a, ⊲) = Soc(S(a, ⊲)) and Ann(a, ⊲) =
Ann(S(a, ⊲)). In particular, if a is nilpotent, then (a, ⊲) is right nilpotent if and
only if S(a, ⊲) is right nilpotent.
Proof. The first part of the statement follows from the fact that W (a) = a whenever
a ⊲ a = 0, which in particular is the case when a ∈ Fix(a, ⊲) or a ∈ Soc(a, ⊲). The
second part of the statement now follows from [1, Lemma 5.3 and Lemma 5.4] and
the analogous statement for post-Lie algebras.                                    
     We are now ready to prove Theorem 1.5.
Proof of Theorem 1.5. Let (a, ⊲) be a post Lie p-ring of L-nilpotency class k. We
can consider (a, ⊲) as a complete connected post-Lie Z-algebra as in Example 6.3.
Since k < p, it follows from a similar argument as used in the proof of Proposi-
tion 5.6 that this filtration also makes (a, +) into a Q-module and the bilinear map
a◦ × a → a is also a bilinear map of Q-modules. We conclude that (a, ⊲) becomes
a complete post-Lie Q-algebra.
   Conversely, let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew p-brace of L-nilpotency class k. By Example 7.2
we find that the filtration Li (A) makes it into a complete connected skew Z-brace.
From Proposition 5.6 it follows that (A, ·, ◦) is a strict complete connected skew
Q-brace.
   The first part of the statement now follows from Theorem 8.19 and the observa-
tion that the order of an element is preserved by the Lazard correspondence.
   At last, recall that any skew brace of order pk is left nilpotent by [12, Proposition
4.4] hence it is L-nilpotent.                                                          

               9. Differentiation in non-zero characteristic
   Recall that a primitive n-th root of unity of a ring R is an element ξ ∈ R such
that ξ n = 1 and ξ k − 1 not a zero divisor for 1 ≤ k < n.
Lemma 9.1. Let R be a ring, let M, N be R-modules, ξ ∈ R a primitive n-th root
of unity where n is invertible in R, and f : M → N a map such that for every
m ∈ M there exist elements α0 , ..., αd ∈ N , with d < n, such that
                       f (rm) = α0 + rα1 + r2 α2 + ... + rd αd .
       P n−1
Then n1 i=0 ξ ik f (ξ −i m) = αk for all 1 ≤ k ≤ d.
Proof. Evaluating the formula yields

Although not stated explicitly, it is clear that this differentiation technique plays a

skew brace setting.
Proposition 9.2. Let pk be a prime power, ξ ∈ Z/pk Z a primitive p − 1-th root

moreover (A, ·) is a filtered group with finite filtration A = A0 = A1 ⊇ ... ⊇ Ap = 1
and such that Ai ∗ Aj ⊆ Ai+j for all i, j ≥ 1. Then

   Note that a filtration as in Proposition 9.2 exists precisely if A{p} = 1 where
 {1}
A     = A and A{k+1} is the subgroup of (A, ·) generated by all a ∗ b and aba−1 b−1
where a ∈ A{i} , b ∈ A{k+1−i} , 1 ≤ i ≤ k. For braces this is precisely the chain of
ideals A[k] used to define strong nilpotency as in [33].
   We remark that there is one potential advantage of the above way of differenti-
ating when working over characteristic pk ; namely that we can have terms of degree
more that p, whereas in the formulas for exp and log these terms are not allowed
since the coefficients of degree p or more do not exist. Indeed, the field Fpn for
example has a primitive (pn − 1)-th root of unity. In particular, this means that
there are possible uses in the case p = 2. It would be very interesting to see whether
this idea of differentiation indeed has some meaningful application in such cases.
In particular, the following question is natural to ask:
                                                                     n

primitive (pn − 1)-th root of unity in Fpn . Does the operation
